With all the talk about Windows 10, 8, and 7 being overly intrusive and harvesting customer data and other issues I'm seriously thinking of switching over to Linux. I see a lot of discussion about the benefits of switching, but what are the downsides? I'm a pretty avid gamer so I'm kind of worried about being able to play my PC games, will switching over be difficult for me? Is the system easy to get used to if all you have used is windows?
What are the downsides of switching to Linux?

For me, the biggest drawback is learning the new OS as well as I know the old one (been using WIndows since the 3.11 days). Also, there are various programs I use which are only available in Windows. I assume that I could run a Windows VM on Linux (or an emulator) and get my programs to work, but it seems overly complicated considering my use case. I assume an emulator would also take some resources, so your rig might not be as fast/good for gaming (someone who uses Linux can advise on this).
The excitement of unlimited potential makes you become a Linux advocate.

what are the downsides?

Sometimes it takes a while until there are good drivers for new hardware.

I'm kind of worried about being able to play my PC games

Linux has a lot fewer AAA games which are officially supported. And emulationg them in wine can be a pain. But you can check what runs before switching the OS or dual boot.

Is the system easy to get used to if all you have used is windows?

An XFCE or KDE or Gnome desktop is quite similar. And With a bit of googling you find lots of help to all sorts.

Linux is easy enough to use, especially if you choose an easy distro. The main downside is indeed the lack of games. I get only 30/138 games from my steam library in linux. Getting used to the different software should not take as long, some of the alternatives are not as mature as or lack some features compared to their MS counterparts however. Specifically LibreOffice being less feature rich the last time I checked (which is some years ago, so it might have improved).

You can always go for both OS's and just choose at boot time.
The downside is that people exaggerate how good or how easy it is to do anything. Just dual boot or run it off a usb drive.

A bunch of Linux geeks here will tell you that it's the shit, switch to it right away. But in reality, look at the numbers. Linux runs on like 10% of world computers, if that, and 99% of those are work computers. Linux has some great things about it, but it is not made for home use no matter what some people try to say. You can forget about basic things working out of the box, like hooking up devices into your pc, most likely you'll run into a problem. Need to run a program that has 100 variations on windows? On Linux you'll probably have to code it up yourself. But honestly don't take my words for it, do what the other person mentioned here, dual boot, and you'll see what we're talking about.

As far as gaming goes, you can run most stuff on a VM if you don't mind the performance hit. Works perfectly fine for anything that doesn't require the latest-and-greatest hardware. A lot of newer games coming out on Steam are linux-compatible out of the gate and I imagine with the advent of Windows 10 a lot of people will be making the switch, spurring on further support by game developers.

Game library will shrink a good deal but a lot of indie and not so indie devs are porting or developing directly for linux these days. Biggest con is that you will have to learn a new OS if you want to do some of the more technical things and you will have to learn new security measures(like being careful of mindlessly copy and pasting commands from help articles) a lot of the same security knowledge applies in linux as well.

Its actually quite easy to get used to since you can have any sort of UI that you want. So if you want something that is W8/7 ish you can use the latest Gnome or even Unity.

You can get a no OS pc on ebay for less than $50. Put a linux distro on there and you are set. Use windows machine for gaming or whatever program you need windows for and Linux machine for everything else.

You can get really fancy and get a KVM switch so you can switch between PCs with one button and use the same Mouse, Keyboard and monitor.

Itunes doesn't work. Not all printers are supported. Lots of familiar apps are gone. I have a dual boot box, and use Linux regularly, but unless you are fanatical about, you can't do everything on Linux that you can do on Windows.

Compatibility and convenience. I'm kind of a flip side of this whole story: I exclusively ran Linux on my desktops from 1994 to around 2006 and now run Windows on my desktop machines. I finally decided to switch to Windows when I realized Windows XP was stable enough to use as a desktop, good enough tools existed on Windows to allow me to remotely work on my Linux development and server machines just as well as from a Linux desktop, and that I was spending way too much time trying to find workarounds for Windows apps that weren't available natively on Linux.

Having said that, the majority of the "computers" I use run Linux. All of my servers at work run Linux, I develop embedded systems that run on Linux, and I use Linux for my media server at home. But I just don't see the point of running a Linux desktop.
